passage:
"I'm the fastest in the whole building. I'll beat you to the gate by a mile."
"Mridul, I'm twelve. You're eight."
"So? I beat Chintu yesterday. And Chintu's fast."
"Chintu is five."
"Doesn't matter. I'm definitely winning. One hundred percent."
Kiran didi tied her laces. "Okay. Ready, steady..."
"GO!" Mridul shot off before she finished.
Halfway across the compound, Kiran passed him easily. She was leaning on the gate when he arrived, red-faced.
"You... you started early!"
"You started early, Mridul."
He stood there panting, mouth open. "But I was sure. I was so sure."
"Being sure isn't the same as being fast," Kiran said, and ruffled his hair. "Want to practise tomorrow?"
He kicked a pebble. "...Maybe."

qa.q: Who did Mridul beat the day before?
qa.a: He beat Chintu, who is five.

qa.q: Why was Mridul so stunned at the gate?
qa.a: He felt shocked and embarrassed, because he had been completely sure he would win and his loud confidence had never been tested against someone faster.

qa.q: How does Kiran help Mridul after the race?
qa.a: She gently says being sure isn't the same as being fast and offers to practise with him, turning the loss into a chance to get better.

qa.q: What is it like for Kiran when Mridul says she started early?
qa.a: Kiran seems amused rather than upset, calmly pointing out that he was the one who started early and staying kind.

grounding: A young boy is completely sure he will win a race against an older cousin and is stunned when he loses.

passage: Last week in GK period, Ma'am asked, "What is the capital of Australia?" My hand shot up so fast my elbow hit Lokesh. "Sydney!" I said, loud, like it was obvious. I was so sure I didn't even think. Ma'am said, "Not quite. Anyone else?" Lokesh said, very softly, "Canberra?" and he was right. My ears went hot. I kept thinking, but I KNEW it. I had seen Sydney in a cartoon with the big white building by the water, so it just felt like the answer. Now I think knowing something feels different from just seeing it a lot. Next time Ma'am asks, I'm going to count to three first. Maybe Saurabh can be loud and right, not only loud.

qa.q: What answer did Lokesh give?
qa.a: Canberra, and he was right.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel so sure the answer was Sydney?
qa.a: Saurabh had seen Sydney in a cartoon, so it felt familiar and certain; being wrong in front of everyone left Saurabh embarrassed, with hot ears.

qa.q: What does Saurabh plan to try next time, and why might it help?
qa.a: Counting to three before answering, which gives time to check whether the answer is really known or just familiar.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt answering softly after Saurabh's loud guess?
qa.a: Lokesh may have felt shy or unsure, speaking quietly after such a confident answer, and then pleased to be right.

grounding: A child recalls blurting a wrong answer with total certainty because it felt familiar, and being stunned when a quiet classmate was right.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Sports Day practice, Thursday
Samir (Class 4) told everyone before the long jump trial that he would "definitely jump the farthest, even farther than Class 5." He did not warm up and laughed when I asked him to check his run-up. He fouled his first two jumps by stepping over the board, and his third was the shortest in the group. Lakshmi, who had practised her run-up all week, won. Samir stood at the pit with his mouth open, then said the sand was "too soft today." He did not want to talk. After the others left, I asked him to show me his run-up, and we measured it together with a tape. He counted his steps out loud. We will practise again on Monday.

qa.q: How did Samir foul his first two jumps?
qa.a: He stepped over the board.

qa.q: Why did Samir blame the sand after the trial?
qa.a: He felt stunned and embarrassed, because he had been sure he would jump farthest, so blaming the sand was easier than admitting he hadn't prepared.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: The teacher measured Samir's run-up with him and had him count his steps, turning loud confidence into real practice.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about her win?
qa.a: Lakshmi likely feels proud and satisfied, because her week of practising the run-up paid off.

grounding: A PE teacher records a boy who was certain he would win the long jump, skipped his warm-up and was stunned to come last.

passage: After two slow rounds of the mustard field on Chacha's motorbike, Anand announced at dinner that he could ride to the Thursday haat himself. "It's easy. Clutch, gear, go." His cousin Afreen raised an eyebrow. "In the field, with Chacha holding the back?" "That was just the first time." On Thursday morning he wheeled the bike into the lane while everyone was at the well. The lane had a bullock cart, three goats and a curve by the pond that the field did not. At the curve he braked too hard, the bike wobbled, and his foot went into the ditch. Afreen, who had followed on foot, grabbed the handlebar. "Keys," she said. Anand handed them over, shaking. That evening Chacha put the keys on the high shelf.

qa.q: What did the lane have that the field did not?
qa.a: A bullock cart, three goats and a curve by the pond.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel ready to ride to the haat?
qa.a: He felt confident because two slow rounds in the field felt easy, so he mistook a little practice for real skill.

qa.q: What would have been a wiser next step for Anand?
qa.a: Keep practising in the field with Chacha and wait until an adult agrees he is ready, instead of taking the bike onto the lane alone.

qa.q: What was it like for Afreen to follow Anand on foot?
qa.a: Afreen was probably worried about him, which is why she followed and grabbed the handlebar the moment he wobbled.

grounding: A teenage boy believes two easy rounds in a field mean he can ride a motorbike, until the real lane proves harder.

passage: Hiroshi had listened to the sonata so many times on the train to school in Osaka that he could hum every note. "I'm basically ready," he told his piano teacher, and when she asked him to rate himself for the spring recital, he wrote 9 out of 10. Camila, who practised in the room after him, wrote 5. On recital day Camila played carefully, slowing at the hard bit, and finished clean. Hiroshi sat down, played the first page beautifully, and then his hands stopped. He knew how the next part sounded. He could hear it perfectly. His fingers had no idea where to go. He started the line again, then again, then skipped to the end. Afterwards Camila found him behind the stage. "Listening isn't the same as playing," he muttered, before she could say anything.

qa.q: What rating did Hiroshi give himself?
qa.a: 9 out of 10.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi rate himself so high before the recital?
qa.a: He felt confident because the sonata was so familiar from the train that recognising it felt like being able to play it.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi do to test himself before the next recital?
qa.a: Play the whole piece from memory for someone a week before, without stopping, to see where his fingers actually get lost.

qa.q: How might Camila see her own lower rating after the recital?
qa.a: Camila may feel quietly relieved that her careful 5 matched a steady performance, and sympathetic toward Hiroshi.

grounding: A teenage boy rates his piano piece highly because he has heard it so often, then cannot play it from memory at the recital.

passage: Last spring I applied to exactly one master's programme. Kamal, my friend from the lab, kept asking, "Jaya, where's your backup?" and I kept laughing. I had the grades, the professor's letter, the project. In my head I had already chosen a hostel room from the photos. I didn't write a single other application, and I told my parents not to worry. The rejection email came on a Tuesday at 3 p.m. I read it four times, sure it was a mistake. It wasn't. What hurt most wasn't only the no. It was that I had nowhere to put it. I had never let myself think "maybe," so the no landed on bare ground. This year I have a list of five, and a paragraph for each that starts, "If this fails..."

qa.q: How many programmes did Jaya apply to last spring?
qa.a: Exactly one master's programme.

qa.q: Why did the rejection hurt Jaya so much?
qa.a: Jaya felt crushed and shocked because doubt had never been allowed in, so there was no plan or thought ready to soften the no.

qa.q: What is Jaya doing differently this year, and why does it help?
qa.a: Applying to five programmes and writing an "If this fails" paragraph for each, which leaves room for error before any result arrives.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt when the rejection came?
qa.a: Kamal may have felt sad for Jaya and perhaps frustrated that the question about a backup had been laughed off.

grounding: A young adult recalls being so sure of one application that no backup was made, so the rejection hurt far more.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Dharamshala, 22 September
Tenzin (second year) organised the class trek and was completely certain it would go well. When I asked about a rain plan, he said, "It won't rain, I've done this trail twice." He booked no shelter, packed no extra ponchos and told the group there was no need to check the forecast. Shalini, his co-organiser, suggested a later date as backup; he laughed it off. The storm came at noon. The group turned back, soaked, and two students' phones died. Tenzin came to my office in the evening and sat for a long time without speaking. Then he said, "I didn't even think it could go wrong." I stayed with him, and we listed what a backup plan would have needed. He asked if he could share the list with the class tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say when asked about a rain plan?
qa.a: He said it wouldn't rain because he had done the trail twice.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin sit so long without speaking?
qa.a: He felt shaken and ashamed, because he had never let himself imagine the trek going wrong, so the storm hit him harder.

qa.q: What did the warden do that helped, and what could Tenzin do next time?
qa.a: The warden stayed and listed what a backup plan would need; next time Tenzin could check the forecast and keep Shalini's later date ready.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel after the storm?
qa.a: Shalini may feel frustrated that the backup date was laughed off, but also sorry for Tenzin.

grounding: A warden records a student who was so sure a trek would go well that he left no backup, and was shaken when it failed.

passage:

passage: At the design agency in Buenos Aires, the client wanted the new website live before their product launch. Kaito, three months into the job, didn't hesitate. "Two weeks. Easy. I've built bigger ones." The room went quiet. Marta, who had seen deadlines slip before, muttered that he should be taken off the job if he missed it. Someone else just wrote "2 weeks" on the board. Camila, the lead, capped the marker. "Kaito, I believe you want this. Help me with three numbers: if nothing goes wrong, if a normal amount goes wrong, and if the client changes the menu twice like last time." Kaito paused. "Two weeks. Three. Maybe five." Camila wrote all three on the board. "We'll tell the client three to five. Check in with me every Friday."

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when Kaito promised two weeks?
qa.a: Camila seems hopeful about Kaito's keenness but cautious, wanting numbers rather than either punishing him or trusting the promise blindly.

qa.q: Which response to Kaito worked best, and why?
qa.a: Camila's request for three numbers, because it turned his certainty into a range the client could rely on, without shaming him as Marta wanted.

qa.q: How might Kaito see the Friday check-ins?
qa.a: He may feel supported rather than doubted, since his estimate was taken seriously and he has a regular place to raise problems.

grounding: A team lead responds to a new colleague's total assurance by asking for a range and a worst case, avoiding both punishment and blind trust.

passage: About a year ago, after a string of confident calls that went wrong, I started a notebook. Every Monday I wrote three predictions about work with a number beside each: "Client signs by month end, 80%." "New intern ready to lead the Friday call by March, 60%." Every month, Swati from accounts and I went through them over tea and ticked right or wrong. It was humbling. When I said 90% about deadlines, I was right only about half the time. But my 70% guesses about people, whether a colleague would enjoy a task or clash with a client, were right almost every time. So now I pad my deadline promises and trust my read on people a bit more. Swati calls it "Maria's weather report."

qa.q: How often was Maria right when saying 90% about deadlines?
qa.a: Only about half the time.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when checking the notebook with Swati?
qa.a: Maria felt humbled on seeing that confident deadline calls were often wrong, but also reassured that guesses about people were reliable.

qa.q: What could someone copy from Maria's notebook habit?
qa.a: Writing predictions with a percentage, checking them regularly with someone else, and adjusting wherever confidence runs too high.

qa.q: How does Swati seem to see the habit?
qa.a: Swati seems to enjoy it and treat it warmly, joking that it is Maria's weather report.

grounding: A young professional recalls writing predictions with percentages, checking them monthly and learning where sure feelings could be trusted.

passage:
Supervisor's note, forecasting team, Kochi, end of quarter
I want to record what Elizabeth has done since January. After her delivery-date estimates missed twice, she began a simple sheet: each estimate, a percentage for how sure she felt, and the actual result filled in later. Today she walked me through three months of it. When she wrote 95%, she was right about two times in three. When she wrote 60%, she was right about six times in ten, almost exactly. She said, "My high numbers are the ones fooling me." Afreen, who sits next to her, has started a sheet of her own. I've asked Elizabeth to show the method at Friday's team meeting, and I will ask everyone to try it for one quarter.

qa.q: How often was Elizabeth right when she wrote 95%?
qa.a: About two times in three.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's line about her high numbers suggest she feels?
qa.a: She seems surprised but grateful, having found that her strongest feelings of certainty were the least reliable.

qa.q: Why is asking the team to try the sheet for a quarter a sensible next step?
qa.a: It spreads a habit that shows people where their confidence can be trusted, based on real results rather than feelings.

qa.q: Why might Afreen have started a sheet of her own?
qa.a: Afreen probably watched Elizabeth's results up close and felt curious or encouraged to check her own confidence.

grounding: A supervisor records a young analyst tracking her predictions with percentages and learning which levels of certainty were reliable.

passage:

Month three of my prediction diary. Tonight's check. On Monday I wrote: "Mango kulfi sells out by 8 p.m., 85% sure." It sold out at 7:40. Tick. "Hrithik manages the tandoor alone on Wednesday, 90%." passage: Kashish, sit. You think those chess videos make you ready to argue with your coach? Let your Tanvir mama tell you something. At sixteen I watched maybe a dozen videos on openings. grounding: An uncle recalls how, at sixteen, a few chess videos made him feel more expert than his coach, until a real game exposed the gaps.

passage: The debate was at ten, and Hemant's partner had phoned in sick at eight, so he would have to speak alone. He wasn't worried. passage: After one week of the soil-health module at the agriculture college in Dharwad, Varun felt he could fix any farm. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potash: he had the chart in his pocket. passage: After the lecture on hypothesis testing at her university in Istanbul, Nour felt unstoppable. She ran through the worksheet in twenty minutes and told her study partner Zeynep, "Honestly, statistics is just following five steps." On Thursday the professor handed out real data from a hospital study: missing values, two groups of different sizes, a result that looked strong until you noticed the samples weren't random. Nour's five steps gave an answer. It was wrong, and she couldn't even see why. By evening she was ready to drop the elective. Zeynep, a year ahead, laughed kindly. "Last year I cried over that same sheet. On Monday you knew the recipe. Now you're seeing the kitchen." Nour pulled the sheet back out and circled the part she didn't understand.

qa.q: How long did Nour take to finish the first worksheet?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why was Nour ready to drop the elective by Thursday evening?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and embarrassed, because the five steps that made her feel expert gave a wrong answer she couldn't explain.

qa.q: What small step does Nour take at the end, and why does it help?
qa.a: She circles the part she doesn't understand, turning the dip into a clear next thing to learn.

qa.q: How does Zeynep see Nour's struggle?
qa.a: Zeynep sees it as normal and even a good sign, remembering crying over the same sheet a year earlier.

grounding: A student feels expert after one lecture, loses confidence on messy real data, and a friend shows the dip is part of learning.

passage: Deepak, you asked what my first year as an engineer was like. Mostly, I thought I was a fraud. I'm the only woman in our structural team, and every time I solved a load problem in ten minutes, I assumed it must be an easy one. Anyone could do it, I thought. When my senior asked me to explain it to the new hires, I apologised first: "Sorry, this is really basic." Then I watched three of them get stuck on the same beam for an hour. I still didn't believe it. I told myself they were tired. It took my manager showing me the review scores, mine at the top of the batch, for me to say out loud, "Manjula, maybe this is not easy. Maybe you're just good at it." Even saying it felt strange.

qa.q: How long did the new hires get stuck on the same beam?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why did Manjula feel like a fraud in the first year?
qa.a: Manjula felt doubtful and unsure, because the problems felt easy, so it seemed they must be easy for everyone.

qa.q: What could help Manjula judge her skill more accurately?
qa.a: Comparing the work with others' on the same task, like the new hires on the beam, and trusting records such as the review scores.

qa.q: How might the new hires feel when Manjula calls the problem basic?
qa.a: They might feel discouraged or small, struggling for an hour on something described as really basic.

grounding: A skilled young engineer recalls assuming her easy problems were easy for everyone and doubting her own ability.

passage:
Monday. Anjali fixed the payment bug in forty minutes and didn't mention it at stand-up. "It was just a missing check," she told Ganga later. "Anyone would've found it."
Wednesday. The team lead asked who could mentor the two interns. Anjali stayed silent. Ganga nudged her. "You should." "Me? I barely know anything. I just look stuff up." That evening she spent two hours reading about topics she already used every day, sure she had gaps everywhere.
Friday. Ganga forwarded her a message from the other team: they had hunted that same payment bug for two weeks before giving up. Anjali read it three times. "Two weeks?" she said. "I thought it was obvious." Ganga grinned. "It was obvious to you." On Monday Anjali put her name down to mentor the interns.

qa.q: How long had the other team hunted the payment bug?
qa.a: Two weeks before giving up.

qa.q: Why did Anjali stay silent about mentoring?
qa.a: She felt unsure and doubtful of herself, believing she barely knew anything because the problems she solved seemed obvious.

qa.q: What helped Anjali see her skill more clearly?
qa.a: Ganga forwarding the other team's message, which gave a real comparison showing the bug had been hard for others.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Anjali's work?
qa.a: Ganga sees it as genuinely skilled and keeps nudging Anjali, pointing out that the bug was only obvious to Anjali.

grounding: Over a week, a skilled young engineer assumes her quick fix was easy for anyone and doubts herself, until a comparison shows otherwise.

passage: Nazia, you keep saying you're not good enough for the site lead role. Let Vasudha aunty tell you a story. When I was twenty-four, on the dam project, I could read a drawing and spot a mistake in seconds. I thought everyone could. So when I found an error in the spillway plans, I didn't report it for a week. I thought, surely the senior engineers have seen it; who am I? Finally my friend Kamala, a surveyor, dragged me to the chief engineer. He looked at it, went pale, and stopped the pour. Nobody else had seen it. He asked me, "Why did you wait?" I said, "I thought it was obvious." He said, "Only to you." After that I learned to speak up first and doubt later.

qa.q: What did Vasudha find in the spillway plans?
qa.a: An error, which she didn't report for a week.

qa.q: Why did young Vasudha wait a week to report the error?
qa.a: She felt unsure of herself, assuming that what she could see so easily must be obvious to the senior engineers too.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what made it work?
qa.a: Kamala dragging her to the chief engineer, who stopped the pour; a friend's push got the skill heard before doubt could keep it quiet.

qa.q: How might the chief engineer have felt looking at the error?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and worried, going pale, and then grateful that Vasudha had found what nobody else had.

grounding: An older engineer recalls how, as a skilled young engineer, she assumed an error obvious to her was obvious to all and nearly stayed silent.

passage: Divyansh, this is Indu's big mentoring story of the month, so listen. You know the new guy on my team, Faraz? First week, he told everyone our testing process was overkill and he could ship features in half the time. My old manager would have laughed at him in front of everyone. I've seen what that does: people just dig in. So I asked him for a coffee and said, "Walk me through how you'd release the login change, step by step, out loud." He started fast. Build, push, done. I asked, "What happens to users who are logged in when it goes out?" He paused. "And where does the old password data go?" Longer pause. He pulled out his notebook without me saying anything. Two days later, he asked me to review his release plan.

qa.q: What question made Faraz pause first?
qa.a: What happens to users who are logged in when the change goes out.

qa.q: Why did Indu choose a quiet coffee instead of laughing at Faraz?
qa.a: Indu felt wary of ridicule after seeing people dig in when mocked, and wanted Faraz to find the gaps without feeling humiliated.

qa.q: What made Indu's approach work?
qa.a: Asking Faraz to explain the release step by step and posing specific questions, so the gaps showed themselves instead of being pointed out harshly.

qa.q: What might Faraz have felt when he pulled out his notebook?
qa.a: He probably felt humbled and a bit caught out, but not attacked, so he began taking the gaps seriously.

grounding: A mentor describes asking an overconfident newcomer to explain a task step by step so his gaps show, instead of mocking him.

passage: I share a desk row with Trisha at the architecture firm, so I watched her handle Gurpreet's first month. He arrived announcing he could draw any site plan in an afternoon. On his third day, a senior sniggered at his drawing in front of everyone, and Gurpreet just got louder about how good he was. Trisha did something different. She sat with him, put his plan next to a finished one, and pointed to two exact places: the drainage slope and the fire exit width. Then she said, "Explain to me how you'd get from the survey to this, one step at a time." Halfway through, he stopped talking and started erasing. I can't say what he felt, but he stayed late that evening, redrawing, and he didn't brag at lunch the next day.

qa.q: Which two places did Trisha point to on the plan?
qa.a: The drainage slope and the fire exit width.

qa.q: What might Trisha have been thinking when she sat down with Gurpreet?
qa.a: She was probably concerned that the snigger had only made him louder, and hoped calm, specific examples would help him see the gaps himself.

qa.q: Why did Trisha's way work where the senior's snigger failed?
qa.a: Pointing to exact problems and asking for a step-by-step explanation let Gurpreet find his own gaps, while ridicule only made him defend himself.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet react differently to the two approaches?
qa.a: After the snigger he got louder about his skill; after Trisha's questions he started erasing, stayed late redrawing and stopped bragging.

grounding: A colleague describes a mentor using specific examples and a step-by-step explanation to show a newcomer his gaps after ridicule had failed.

passage:
Monday. Rehana, two weeks into the newsroom, told the desk she could write the budget story alone. "It's just numbers." Someone snorted, "Sure, genius," and Rehana crossed her arms and said it again, louder.
Tuesday. Rekha, the senior sub-editor, pulled a chair beside her. She didn't mention the snort. She showed Rehana last year's budget story and pointed to two lines: one where the reporter compared a figure with rising prices, and one where a farmer explained what the change meant for him. "Tell me, step by step, how you'd get from the budget document to lines like these." Rehana began confidently, then slowed. "I'd... read it. And then... I don't know who I'd call."
Thursday. Rehana came to Rekha's desk with a list of five people to phone and a question about prices she had written down herself.

qa.q: What did Rehana bring to Rekha's desk on Thursday?
qa.a: A list of five people to phone and a question about prices she had written down herself.

qa.q: Why did Rehana cross her arms on Monday?
qa.a: She felt mocked and defensive after the snort, so she dug in and repeated her claim more loudly.

qa.q: Which response helped Rehana, and why?
qa.a: Rekha's specific examples and step-by-step question helped, because Rehana found her own gap; the snort only hardened her claim.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Rehana's list on Thursday?
qa.a: Rekha probably feels pleased, since the gaps showed up through Rehana's own explanation and she is now filling them.

grounding: Over a week, a senior editor uses specific examples and a step-by-step question to show a confident newcomer her gaps after mockery failed.

passage: At lunch before the inter-house football final, Harsha had painted a green stripe on his cheek. "Green House will smash Red. Easy three-nil," he told everyone in the canteen queue. Red won two-one. By afternoon assembly, Harsha had wiped the stripe off. "I knew Green would lose," he said to Ayesha. "Their goalkeeper is too short. It was obvious." Ayesha stared at him. "You said three-nil to Green. In the canteen. You even bet me your eraser." "I was joking. I knew all along." Ayesha held out her hand. "Then give me the eraser." Harsha looked at the ceiling, then slowly dug the eraser out of his pencil box.

qa.q: What score did Harsha predict before the final?
qa.a: Three-nil to Green House.

qa.q: Why does Harsha now say he knew Green would lose?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed about his loud prediction, and now that the result is known, the short goalkeeper seems like an obvious sign, so the new story feels true to him.

qa.q: What could help Harsha remember what he really thought before a match?
qa.a: Writing his prediction down before the game and looking at it afterwards, so his memory can't quietly change it.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Harsha's claim?
qa.a: Ayesha finds it unfair and a bit funny, remembering exactly what he said, and asks for the eraser to prove it.

grounding: After the final, a boy claims he knew his team would lose, though he had loudly predicted they would win.

passage:
Friday. Vijay and Saurabh argued on the stairs about Sunday's colony match. "Block B might win, might not," Vijay said. "Their bowler is fast, but our batting is better. Fifty-fifty." Saurabh wrote it on the wall calendar in pencil: V says 50-50.
Sunday. Block B's fast bowler took four wickets, and Vijay's team lost by twenty runs. Vijay threw his cap on the ground.
Tuesday. At school, Vijay told his whole row, "I knew we'd lose. That bowler was always going to finish us. I said it on Friday." Saurabh, sitting behind him, leaned forward. "You said fifty-fifty. It's on the calendar." Vijay frowned. "No, I definitely said we'd lose." That evening he looked at the calendar and read the pencil note twice, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Saurabh write on the wall calendar?
qa.a: V says 50-50.

qa.q: How does Vijay feel when he reads the calendar note?
qa.a: He is probably surprised and a little embarrassed, because he truly believed he had predicted the loss.

qa.q: What does the calendar note show, and how could Vijay use the idea?
qa.a: A written guess can't be rewritten later; Vijay could jot down his predictions before matches to check how sure he really was.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to hear Vijay's story at school?
qa.a: Saurabh is likely amused and a bit annoyed, since he wrote down the fifty-fifty and knows the story has changed.

grounding: Across a few days, a boy's honest fifty-fifty guess turns in his memory into 'I knew we'd lose' after the match.

passage: Wasim, you said you knew your team would lose yesterday. Let your Amandeep uncle tell you about the hockey final at our village mela when I was nine. Before the match, I told everyone our side would win for sure. I even climbed a tree to watch. We lost, four goals to one. Walking home, I told my father, "I knew it. Their centre-forward was too fast. I could see it from the start." My father stopped walking. "Amandeep, this morning you told the whole lane we'd win." I was angry, because in my head I really had known. It felt like a memory, not a story I had just made. My father wasn't cross. He said, "Next time, tell me your guess, and I'll remember it for you." So before every match I told him, and he always remembered.

qa.q: What was the score of the hockey final?
qa.a: Four goals to one.

qa.q: Why was young Amandeep angry when his father reminded him?
qa.a: He felt caught out and confused, because the new story felt like a real memory, so he believed he had known all along.

qa.q: What choice did the father make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Instead of scolding, he offered to remember Amandeep's guesses before each match, so the real prediction could be checked afterwards.

qa.q: How might the father have seen Amandeep's claim on the walk home?
qa.a: He likely found it gently funny, knowing the boy had told the whole lane they would win, and chose to help rather than scold.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at nine, he claimed he knew his team would lose, though he had predicted a win that morning.
